title: Boden's Mate
subtitle: Criss-cross bishops demolish the castled king (London, 1853).
goals: Sacrifice the queen to open the diagonal

steps.say: London, 1853: Schulder has just castled queenside against Samuel Boden — straight into immortality. Boden's Mate kills a queenside-castled king with two bishops slicing across each other like scissors. The trigger is always the same: a queen sacrifice on c3 (or c6) to rip open the king's diagonal. You're playing Black. Watch the c3 pawn.

steps.prompt: Warm up with the pattern from the White side: the black king castled long, and your bishops point at him from BOTH diagonals. Rip the cover off!
hints: Count your attackers on c6: the queen hits it, and after it falls, the f1 bishop's diagonal to a6 opens with deadly effect.
Sacrifice the queen on c6! The recapture is forced — and then Ba6 is mate: one bishop checks, the other seals b8.

line.say: The Boden sacrifice — the queen dies to drag the b7 pawn off its diagonal...
The scissors close: Ba6 checks along the freshly opened diagonal while your f4 bishop covers b8. Two minor pieces, one dead king, queen well spent.

rejections.say: One blade of the scissors — but bxa6 just takes it: the b7 pawn still guards the diagonal. The QUEEN must remove that pawn first, by force: Qxc6+!

steps.wrongSay: The b7 pawn is the king's whole roof. Which forcing sacrifice makes it move?
steps.successSay: Queen sac on c6, mate with the bishops — the Boden formula against every long-castled king.

steps.prompt: Now the real thing, exactly as Boden played it in 1853. White just castled long — find the five-move demolition. It starts with a quiet center break!
hints: Your f8 bishop dreams of a3 — but your OWN d6 pawn blocks its diagonal. One pawn move fixes that and attacks a bishop at the same time.
d5! clears the f8–a3 diagonal with tempo. Then Qxc3+!! forces bxc3, and Ba3# closes the scissors with the f5 bishop covering b1.

line.say: The point most players miss: this clears your OWN bishop's path to a3 — and it attacks the c4 bishop, so White has no time to react.
THE queen sacrifice. The c3 pawn was the king's last shield — and now it must capture, opening the a3–c1 diagonal...
Boden's Mate, London 1853. The a3 bishop checks, the f5 bishop covers b1 and d3 — criss-cross. This exact picture has ended thousands of games since; now you've played the original.

rejections.say: bxc3 — and now Ba3+ is impossible: your OWN d6 pawn blocks the f8-bishop's diagonal! The queen died for nothing. First d5!, clearing the diagonal with tempo, THEN the sacrifice. Move order is the whole combination.

steps.wrongSay: Two steps: deflect the c4 bishop with a pawn break, then sacrifice the queen on c3.
steps.successSay: A deflection, a queen sac, and a criss-cross mate — 1853's finest, played by you.

steps.say: Remember the anatomy: against a king castled long, the squares b8 and the b7-pawn's diagonal are the two weak beams. One bishop aims at each. Any forcing move that removes the b-pawn — usually a queen sacrifice on c6 or c3 — brings the whole roof down. From today, every long-castled king you face should make you glance at those diagonals.
